strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: high-fidelity, localized generative editing of explicit 3D meshes, in contrast to the more heavily studied NeRF/3DGS editing literature.

The proposed image-edit → mesh-generate → seamless-fusion pipeline is a sensible decomposition that leverages mature 2D editing models and 3D generation models rather than trying to solve everything end-to-end, which is a pragmatic engineering contribution.

The Joint Geometry and Appearance Fusion module, combining a hybrid SDF/Mesh representation with Poisson-style normal blending and texture harmonization losses (distribution alignment, gradient preservation, boundary smoothing), is reasonably well motivated and each component is ablated both qualitatively and quantitatively (Fig. 6, Tab. 2).
Demonstrated versatility across text-driven insertion/deletion and drag-based editing (Fig. 5) suggests the framework generalizes beyond a single editing modality.
Qualitative results in Fig. 4 show visibly richer local detail and more harmonious boundaries than the three baselines on the presented examples.
weaknesses: Evaluation is very limited in scale: only six objects comprise the entire benchmark, with no stated per-category breakdown, no standard deviations/confidence intervals, and no user study to corroborate perceptual claims of 'high fidelity,' which is a fairly strong claim for such a small test set.

The method depends heavily on multiple proprietary/black-box off-the-shelf tools (FLUX Kontext, MeshyAI, LightningDrag), which limits reproducibility; MeshyAI in particular is a paid closed API, and exact prompts/parameters used for these external tools are not reported, making it hard for others to replicate results.

The core technical novelty is incremental: the geometry blending re-purposes MagicClay's SDF/mesh hybrid representation with a Poisson-blended normal-map supervision signal, and the texture harmonization combines several previously known losses (KDE-based distribution matching, gradient preservation à la Poisson image editing, distance-weighted boundary loss) — the individual pieces are largely adaptations of existing techniques rather than fundamentally new formulations.

No runtime/scalability comparison against baselines is provided (only self-reported timings for the two blending stages), and no discussion of failure cases beyond the two 'Fail' entries in Fig. 4, which are not analyzed in text (why FocalDreamer fails on those two examples is not discussed, nor is a failure case of the proposed method shown).

The pipeline requires several manual/semi-manual steps (rendering a reference view, selecting the edited region, aligning meshes, extracting intersection regions with threshold hyperparameters ϵ0, ϵ1), and there is no analysis of sensitivity to these thresholds or to viewpoint selection for the reference render, raising concerns about robustness to different objects/poses.

The user-study-free CLIP/NIQE/NIMA quantitative metrics, while standard, are known to correlate imperfectly with true geometric fidelity (which is the central claim of the paper); no explicit geometric fidelity metric (e.g., Chamfer distance to a ground-truth edited shape, or geometry-focused perceptual metrics) is reported despite geometry preservation being a headline contribution.

The paper does not report failure modes or limitations of the Poisson Geometry/Texture blending itself (e.g., when generated edited-region mesh topology strongly diverges from the reference mesh, or when boundary regions are highly non-planar), leaving open questions about robustness for more complex real-world editing tasks.

Related-work coverage of concurrent/prior mesh-specific generative editing baselines is somewhat limited to three methods (FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit); it is unclear whether these are truly the strongest currently available baselines, and no ablation against simpler alternatives to Poisson-based blending (e.g. Laplacian-based mesh blending) is provided to isolate the Poisson formulation's specific benefit versus other classical smoothing/blending techniques.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored problem (generative mesh-level editing with explicit surface preservation) relative to the more heavily studied NeRF/Gaussian editing literature.
The image-editing -> mesh-generation -> seamless-fusion pipeline is a sensible way to leverage complementary strengths of mature 2D editing and 3D generation models without retraining either.

Poisson Geometry Blending (normal blending in the SDF/mesh hybrid representation) and Poisson Texture Harmonization (gradient + boundary + distribution-aware losses) are reasonable, non-trivial extensions of classical Poisson image editing to the mesh domain, and the paper offers a plausible complexity argument (O(kn^2) vs O(n^3)) for why this is more tractable than naive 3D Poisson solving.

Ablation studies (Table 2, Fig. 6) isolate the contribution of each proposed component (geometry blending, texture harmonization, and individual loss terms), which supports the claimed design choices.

Demonstrates versatility by extending the framework to drag-based editing in addition to text-driven editing, and shows backbone-agnosticism (Trellis, Hunyuan3D 2.5, MeshyAI) achieving comparable performance, which strengthens the claim that gains come from the fusion method rather than a specific generator.
Quantitative results consistently outperform four recent baselines (FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit, VoxHammer) across CLIP-based and no-reference quality metrics.
weaknesses: No human/user study is reported despite the central claims being about perceptual seamlessness and 'harmonious' visual fusion; the chosen metrics (CLIPsim, CLIPdir, NIQE, NIMA) are weak proxies for the specific quality (seamless boundary blending) the paper is designed to achieve.

The pipeline depends on a proprietary, closed-source image-to-mesh generator (MeshyAI) for the main reported results, which limits reproducibility; open backbones (Trellis, Hunyuan3D) are only used in a smaller ablation.

Dataset construction details are thin: no information on how the 100 models were selected/curated, how editing prompts were chosen, or how consistent the 3-prompts-per-model protocol is across methods, making it hard to judge evaluation breadth and fairness.

Failure cases (two instances marked 'Fail' in Fig. 4 for baselines) are not analyzed for the proposed method itself; there is little discussion of where CraftMesh's own pipeline might fail (e.g., extreme topology changes, disconnected components, or when 2D edits are not liftable to consistent 3D geometry).
No runtime or scalability comparison against baselines is provided beyond raw timing of the proposed modules, so it is unclear how compute cost compares to competing pipelines.

Some notational and procedural details (e.g., precise criteria for extracting intersection regions, boundary width parameter tuning, robustness of mesh Boolean operations on non-manifold or noisy meshes) are underspecified, which could hinder faithful reproduction.

The method's dependence on successful mesh Boolean operations and reference-mesh alignment is a potential brittleness point that is not stress-tested on the messy, real-world meshes the introduction motivates the work with.
